Let  $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\binom{[n]}{d+1}$  be a  $(d+1)$ -uniform set system over the ground set  $[n]\overset{\rm{def}}{=}\{1,\dots,n\}$ . The Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension (VC-dimension) of  $\mathcal{F}$ , denoted as  $\textup{VC}(\mathcal{F})$  is defined to be the size of the largest set  $S\subseteq[n]$  such that every subset of  $S$  is realized as an intersection  $S\cap F$  for some  $F\in\mathcal{F}$ , i.e. for all  $S^{\prime}\subseteq S$ , there exists  $F\in\mathcal{F}$  such that  $S^{\prime}=S\cap F$ .
Since every set family  $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\binom{[n]}{d+1}$  has VC-dimension at most  $d+1$ , it is natural to ask for the maximum size of  $\mathcal{F}$  with VC-dimension at most  $d$ . Frankl and Pach [8] proved that any such set family has size at most  $\binom{n}{d}$ . Then Frankl and Pach [8] and Erdős [5] conjectured that the upper bound can be improved to  $\binom{n-1}{d}$  when  $n$  is large enough. However, Ahlswede and Khachatrian constructed a counterexample of size  $\binom{n-1}{d}+\binom{n-4}{d-2}$ , and this was later generalized by Mubayi and Zhao [10] where they constructed a class of constructions attaining the same size. The upper bound was recently improved to  $\binom{n-1}{d}+O_{d}(n^{d-2})$  by Yang and Yu [12], matching the second order term of the family constructed in [10] up to a multiplicative constant. For more works along this line, see [4, 9, 11].
Notice that in the case when  $\mathcal{F}$  is a  $(d+1)$ -uniform family, we can equivalently formulate the condition that  $\textup{VC}(\mathcal{F})\leqslant d$  as follows: for each  $F\in\mathcal{F}$ , there exists a subset  $B_{F}\subseteq F$  such that for any  $F^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}$ , we have  $F\cap F^{\prime}\neq B_{F}$ . We call  $B_{F}$  a witness of  $F$  in the sense that it cannot be realized as an intersection of  $F$  with any set  $F^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}$ . In this note, we are interested in the case where all witness sets  $B_{F}$  have the same size.
Definition 1.1 ( $s$ -witness family).
Let  $n\geqslant d+1$  and  $0\leqslant s\leqslant d$ . A family  $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\binom{[n]}{d+1}$  is an  $s$ -witness family if it satisfies the following condition: for every  $F\in\mathcal{F}$ , there exists  $B_{F}\subseteq F$  of size  $s$  such that  $F\cap F^{\prime}\neq B_{F}$  for every  $F^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}$ .
A  $0$ -witness family  $\mathcal{F}$  is exactly an intersecting family since we have  $F\cap F^{\prime}\neq\varnothing$  for all  $F,F^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}$ . The well-known Erdős–Ko–Rado Theorem states the following upper bound for intersecting families.
Theorem 1.2 (Erdős–Ko–Rado [6]).
Let  $d\geqslant 0$  and  $n\geqslant 2(d+1)$ . If  $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\binom{[n]}{d+1}$  is an intersecting family, then  $|\mathcal{F}|\leqslant\binom{n-1}{d}$ . Moreover, when  $n>2(d+1)$ , equality holds if and only if  $\mathcal{F}$  is a star.
As a generalization of the Erdős–Ko–Rado Theorem, the first author, Xu, Yip, and Zhang made the following conjecture in [4].
Conjecture 1.3 ([4]).
Let  $n\geqslant 2(d+1)$  and  $0\leqslant s\leqslant d$ . Suppose  $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\binom{[n]}{d+1}$  is an  $s$ -witness family. Then  $|\mathcal{F}|\leqslant\binom{n-1}{d}$ .
It is clear that when  $s=0$ , Conjecture 1.3 follows from Theorem 1.2. In [4], the authors confirmed Conjecture 1.3 in the case where  $s\in\{1,d\}$  and  $n$  is sufficiently large. Moreover, they showed that equality holds if and only if  $\mathcal{F}$  is a star when  $s\in\{1,d\}$  and remarked that it might be plausible to conjecture that the maximum set families achieving the bound in Conjecture 1.3 must be stars for all  $0\leqslant s\leqslant d$ .
In this note, we prove Conjecture 1.3 in the case when  $s\leqslant d/2$  and  $n$  is sufficiently large.
Theorem 1.4.
Let  $1\leqslant s\leqslant d/2$  and let  $n$  be sufficiently large. Suppose  $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\binom{[n]}{d+1}$  is an  $s$ -witness family. Then  $|\mathcal{F}|\leqslant\binom{n-1}{d}$ . Moreover, if  $|\mathcal{F}|=\binom{n-1}{d}$ , then  $\mathcal{F}$  is a star.
Together with Theorem 1.2 and the results in [4], the remaining open cases of Conjecture 1.3 are when  $d/2<s\leqslant d-1$ . In these remaining open cases, we give a construction that is not a single star achieving the size  $\binom{n-1}{d}$ , illustrating the barriers to adapting current methods as all the proofs of the known cases show that  $\mathcal{F}$  must be a single star if equality is achieved.
Theorem 1.5.
For any  $n\geqslant s+3$  and  $d/2<s\leqslant d-1$ , there exists an  $s$ -witness family  $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\binom{[n]}{d+1}$  of size  $\binom{n-1}{d}$  that is not a star.
We will prove Theorem 1.5 by giving an explicit construction that is contained in the union of two star families but not contained in a single star family. Recall that the piercing number  $\tau(\mathcal{F})$  is the cardinality of the smallest set  $T$  such that  $F\cap T\neq\varnothing$  for all  $F\in\mathcal{F}$ . In particular, the construction given in the proof of Theorem 1.5 has piercing number  $2$ . Furthermore, we can generalize the construction in Theorem 1.5 and get  $s$ -witness families of size  $\binom{n-1}{d}$  with arbitrary large piercing number.
Theorem 1.6.
Let  $d,s,k\geqslant 1$  be integers such that  $d/2<s\leqslant d-k+1$  and  $n\geqslant\max(k+(k-1)s,d+2k-1)$ . There exists an  $s$ -witness family  $\mathcal{F}\subseteq{[n]\choose d+1}$  of size  ${n-1\choose d}$  such that  $\tau(\mathcal{F})=k$ .
We remark that our construction gives several pairwise non-isomorphic examples (up to a permutation of the ground set) proving Theorem 1.5, but the construction for Theorem 1.6 gives only one such example (up to a permutation of the ground set). Therefore, we will present both the proof of Theorem 1.5 and the proof of Theorem 1.6 in Section 3 for completeness despite the fact that they share many similarities.11

Theorem 3.
$\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\hskip 15.0ptp_{n}(1-w)=(-1)^{(n-1)}p_{n}(w).$
Proof.
We will break our collection of LEGO configurations into a number of equivalence classes, each corresponding to a connected red-black graph  $G$  as defined below. A class will consist of:
•
A tuple  $(m_{1},...,m_{k})$  with  $m_{1}+\cdots+m_{k}=n$  where  $m_{i}$  is the number of bricks on the  $i$ th layer. Layers are numbered from the bottom (layer 1) up.
•
For each of the  $m_{1}m_{2}+m_{2}m_{3}+...+m_{k-1}m_{k}$  pairs of bricks on adjacent layers the disjoint possibilities (1) they are joined, (2) the top brick is strictly to the left of the bottom brick, (3) the top brick is strictly to the right of the bottom brick.
Note that here a class is a coarser notion than the notion of type, defined above.
From such data one can construct a directed graph with red and black edges – the vertices correspond to bricks, while edges encode the relative-position constraints between bricks, i.e. horizontal-offset inequalities. One constructs a red edge from the vertex corresponding to the brick furthest to the right to the vertex of the brick to the left in cases (1) and (3), and constructs a black edge going both ways in case (2). For any two adjacent bricks on the same layer, one is constrained to lie strictly to the right of the other, and we similarly add a red edge to enforce this constraint.
Note also that such a directed graph restricted to its black edges is strongly connected, as our LEGO configuration itself is connected.
Expressed more formally as follows, we can count structures in a class by points in a polytope as shown below, bringing the problem into the realm of Ehrhart reciprocity [2, 13].
Definition 2.
Consider  $H=(V=\{v_{0},...,v_{n-1}\},E_{B},E_{R})$  a directed graph with black edges (denoted by  $E_{B}$ ) and red edges (denoted by  $E_{R}$ ).
Assume also that  $G$  restricted to its black edges is strongly connected. We call such a graph a connected red - black graph. For  $w>0$  an integer, we let  $g_{H}(w)$  be the number of tuples  $(a_{1},...,a_{n-1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$  satisfying
•
$a_{0}:=0$
•
$a_{i}<a_{j}+w:(i,j)\in E_{B}$
•
$a_{i}\geq a_{j}+w:(i,j)\in E_{R}$
Note that the strong connectedness (i.e, the existence of a directed path in both directions from any vertex to the root) is a sufficient condition for this to be finite: if there is a path of length  $k$  from  $v_{i}$  to  $v_{j}$  we have  $a_{i}<a_{j}+kw$  so in particular for all  $i,$   $|a_{i}|<(n-1)w$ .
If a class corresponds to some graph  $H,$  then  $g_{H}(w)$  counts the number of LEGO configurations in that class. Furthermore,  $p_{n}(w)$  is a sum of functions of the form  $g_{H}(w)$  where  $H$  varies over some connected red - black graphs on  $n$  vertices.
It now suffices to prove that  $g_{H}$  can be extended to a polynomial satisfying  $g_{H}(1-w)=(-1)^{n-1}g_{H}(w)$ .
In full generality this is not yet quite enough for us to use basic Ehrhart duality. However, we can use it in a special case:
Definition 3.
For any strongly connected rooted directed graph  $G=(V,E)$  we can define  $g_{G}$  by considering it to be a connected red-black graph without any red edges, that is, for  $w>0$  an integer, we let  $g_{H}(w)$  be the number of tuples  $(a_{1},...,a_{n-1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$  satisfying
•
$a_{0}:=0$
•
$a_{i}<a_{j}+w:(i,j)\in E_{B}$
We call these connected black graphs.
Lemma 1.
For any connected black graph  $G$ ,  $g_{G}$  may be extended to a polynomial (which we will also call  $g_{G}$  for brevity) satisfying
$g_{G}(1-w)=(-1)^{n-1}g_{G}(w).$
Proof.
Now, the constraints  $x_{i}\leq x_{j}+1$  for  $(v_{i},v_{j})\in E$  carve out an integer polytope  $P_{G}$  in  $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}=\{(x_{1},...,x_{n-1}):x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}\}$  where we define  $x_{0}=0,$  and this is exactly the polytope we dilate.  $P_{G}$  has a nonempty interior (all  $x_{i}=0$  satisfies  $x_{i}\leq x_{j}+1$  strictly), hence a neighbourhood of the origin lies in  $P_{G},$  so it is full-dimensional in  $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}.$
Its Ehrhart polynomials are, for positive integer  $w,$
$L_{P_{G}}(w)=\#\{a\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-1}:a_{i}\leq a_{j}+w\}=g_{G}(w+1),$
since  $a_{i}\leq a_{j}+w$  is  $a_{i}<a_{j}+w+1,$  i.e. the strict-g at argument  $w+1.$  And
$L_{P^{\circ}_{G}}(w)=\#\{a\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-1}:a_{i}<a_{j}+w\}=g_{G}(w).$
Recall that  $P_{G}^{\circ}$  is the interior of  $P_{G}$ .
By Ehrhart duality [13, 2] it is the case that
$L_{P_{G}^{\circ}}(w)=(-1)^{n-1}L_{P_{G}}(-w).$
This gives
$g_{G}(w)=(-1)^{n-1}g_{G}(-w+1)=(-1)^{n-1}g_{G}(1-w).$
By Ehrhart’s theorem  $L_{P_{G}}$  is a polynomial, so  $g_{G}(w)=L_{P_{G}}(w-1)$  agrees with a polynomial for all integers  $w\geq 1;$  we take this polynomial as the extension of  $g_{G}.$
Since these agree for all positive integers  $w$  and both sides are polynomials, the identity holds identically.

2
A more general setting for this kind of identity seems to be convex integer polytopes whose linear programming duals are themselves integer polytopes – this is a pleasing symmetry, but it is unclear to the authors what is known about such objects.
∎
We would like to extend this result from connected black graphs to connected red - black graphs. Fortunately it will turn out that  $g_{H}$  is a linear combination of polynomials of the form  $g_{G}$  for  $G$  a connected black graph.
Lemma 2.
$g_{H}(w)$  is a polynomial satisfying
$g_{H}(1-w)=(-1)^{n-1}g_{H}(w)$
Proof.
By the inclusion - exclusion principle for  $G=(V=\{v_{0},...,v_{n-1}\},E_{B},E_{R})$  we have
$g_{H}(w)=\sum_{T\subseteq E_{R}}(-1)^{|T|}g_{(V,E_{B}\cup T)}(w).$
Because a red edge imposes  $a_{i}\geq a_{j}+w,$  which is the complement of the black constraint  $a_{i}<a_{j}+w\,\,(=a_{i}\leq a_{j}+w-1)$  on that edge - over the integers these two are exactly complementary, with no overlap and no gap. So “red edge satisfied"= “black-version of that edge violated".  $g_{(V,E_{B}\cup T)}$  counts tuples satisfying the black  $E_{B}$  constraints, and the black version of the edges in  $T,$  and the alternating sum over  $T$  sieves out exactly those violating all red edges’ black-versions, i.e. satisfying all the red constraints.
So
$g_{H}(1-w)=\sum_{T}(-1)^{|T|}g_{G_{T}}(1-w)=\sum_{T}(-1)^{|T|}(-1)^{n-1}g_{G_{T}}(w)=(-1)^{n-1}g_{H}(w),$
and so each of the graphs  $G_{T}=(V,E_{B}\cup T)$  satisfy
$g_{G_{T}}(1-w)=(-1)^{n-1}g_{G_{T}}(w)$
That is to say, for each subset  $T$  of the red edges, recolour those red edges as black (turning the red  $a_{i}\geq a_{j}+w$  into the black  $a_{i}\leq a_{j}+w-1$  on that edge), count the resulting all-black graph with  $g,$  and add it with sign  $(-1)^{|T|}.$  Because each summand  $g_{G_{T}}$  satisfies the  $(-1)^{n-1}$  reflection, and the signs  $(-1)^{|T|}$  don’t depend on  $w,$  the whole alternating sum inherits the same reflection symmetry.
∎
Observing that
•
$p_{n}$  is a linear combination of polynomials  $g_{H}$  for  $H$  a connected red - black graph on  $n$  vertices.
•
For any connected red-black graph  $H$  on  $n$  vertices  $g_{H}$  is a linear combination of polynomials  $g_{G}$  for  $G$  a connected black graph on  $n$  vertices.
•
For  $G$  a connected black graph on  $n$  vertices  $g_{G}$  is a polynomial satisfying  $g_{G}(1-w)=(-1)^{n-1}g_{G}(w)$
We conclude that
$p_{n}(1-w)=(-1)^{(n-1)}p_{n}(w).$
∎

4.2. Matrix Ehrhart-Zeta duality
One can extend Ehrhart-Zeta duality in terms of
infinite matrices as follows. For  $k,\ell\in\mathbb{N}$  we denote by  $\nabla_{\tau}(k,\ell)$  the
number of  $k$ -multichains in the poset of
lattice points of  $\ell{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}$  (where the
order is induced from  $\mathbb{N}^{n}$ , as usual). This
function
can be viewed as an infinite matrix with rows
and columns indexed by nonnegative integers,
every column of which is the sequence of values
of a zeta polynomial. We have  $\nabla_{\tau}(k,0)=\nabla_{\tau}(0,\ell)=1$ ,  $\nabla_{\tau}(k,1)={\mathcal{Z}}(P_{\tau},k+1)$  and  $\nabla_{\tau}(1,\ell)={\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},\ell)$  for all  $k,\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ .
The following conjecture generalizes part (b)
of Theorem 1.5; it has been verified
by computer on certain finite pieces of
$\nabla_{\tau}$  for preorders of size at most 5.
Conjecture 4.2.
The matrix  $\nabla_{\tau}$  is the transpose of
$\nabla_{\tau^{\ast}}$  for every preorder  $\tau$ .
A bijective proof of Ehrhart-Zeta duality
was given for chain preorders in [Ath25].
This proof can be easily extended in the setting
of the matrix Ehrhart-Zeta duality. We sketch the
proof of the following proposition, which
generalizes the first proof of
Theorem 1.3 given in
[Ath25, Section 4].
Proposition 4.3.
Conjecture 4.2 holds for all
chain preorders.
Proof.

Definition 3.16.
A conjugacy class  $c\in{\Gamma}_{*}$  is called real (resp. complex)
if  $c=\bar{c}$  (resp.  $c\neq\bar{c}$ ).
Define  ${\Gamma}^{cx}_{*}=\{c\in{\Gamma}_{*}\mid c\neq\bar{c}\}$
and  ${\Gamma}^{re}_{*}=\{c\in{\Gamma}_{*}\mid c\neq c^{0}\text{ and }c=\bar{c}\}.$
Of course, we have  $|{\Gamma}_{*}|=|{\Gamma}^{cx}_{*}|+|{\Gamma}^{re}_{*}|+1$  and
$|{\Gamma}^{cx}_{*}|$  is always an even integer.
Theorem 3.17.
The ring  $\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{G}_{\Gamma}(n)$  for every  $n$  does not depend
on the finite group  ${\Gamma}$ , but depends only on
the two numbers  $|{\Gamma}_{*}|$  and  $|{\Gamma}^{re}_{*}|$ .
In particular, if  $G$  is another finite group
such that  $|{\Gamma}_{*}|=|G_{*}|$  and  $|{\Gamma}^{re}_{*}|=|G^{re}_{*}|$ ,
then the rings  $\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{G}_{\Gamma}(n)$  and
$\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{G}_{G}(n)$  are isomorphic for every  $n$ .
Proof.

the ring  $\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{G}_{\Gamma}(n)$  with respect
to the new basis  $\widetilde{K}_{\lambda}$
no longer depends on the group  ${\Gamma}$ .
Let  $G$  be another finite group
such that  $|{\Gamma}_{*}|=|G_{*}|$  and  $|{\Gamma}^{re}_{*}|=|G^{re}_{*}|$ .
Fix a bijection  $\varphi$  from  ${\Gamma}_{*}$  to  $G_{*}$  such that
its restriction to  ${\Gamma}^{re}_{*}$  is one-to-one and onto
$G^{re}_{*}$ . Then the obvious map by matching
the rescaled conjugacy classes of  ${{\Gamma}_{n}}$  and
those of  $G_{n}$  in terms of  $\varphi$
is a ring isomorphism by Theorems 3.3,
3.4 and Corollary 3.14.

5 Final Remarks
5.1 Open Problems
Numerical evidence suggests that the following holds.
Conjecture 5.1
For every subset  $M\subseteq[0,n-1]$  and  $i\in[\pm n]$  the polynomial
$\sum_{\{\sigma\in B_{n}\,|\,{\it Des}_{B}(\sigma^{-1})\subseteq M,\,\sigma(n)=i\}}q^{\ell_{B}(\sigma)}=\sum_{\{\sigma\in B_{n}\,|\,{\it Des}_{B}(\sigma^{-1})\subseteq M,\,\sigma(n)=i\}}q^{{\it fmaj}(\sigma)}.$
is (symmetric and) unimodal.
Conjecture 5.2
For every subset  $M\subseteq[0,n-1]$  the polynomial
$\sum_{\{\sigma\in B_{n}\,|\,{\it Des}_{B}(\sigma^{-1})\subseteq M\}}q^{\ell_{B}(\sigma)}=\sum_{\{\sigma\in B_{n}\,|\,{\it Des}_{B}(\sigma^{-1})\subseteq M\}}q^{{\it fmaj}(\sigma)}.$
is (symmetric and) unimodal.
Using well known results (see, e.g., [36, Proposition 1 and Theorem 11])
and Theorems 3.3, 4.2 and 4.3, it is easy to see that the above conjectures are equivalent to the following.
Conjecture 5.3
For  $0\leq k<n$  the polynomial
${n\brack k}_{q}\cdot\prod\limits_{j=k+1}^{n}(1+q^{j})$
is (symmetric and) unimodal.
We have verified these conjectures for  $n\leq 15$ . Conjecture 5.3
clearly holds for  $k=n-1$  and is known to be true for  $k=0$  (see, e.g.,

1.1 Non-commutative 1-forms
Let  $A$  be an associative algebra. A 1-form on  $A$  is a finite sum
of the expressions  $a\cdot db\cdot c$ , where  $a,b,c\in A$  modulo the
following two relations:
(i)
the cyclicity:  $t\cdot a\cdot db\cdot c=a\cdot db\cdot c\cdot t$  for any  $a,b,c,t\in A$ ,
(2)
the Leibniz rule:  $d(a\cdot b)=(da)\cdot b+a\cdot db$ .
We say that a 1-form on  $A$  is exact if it has the form  $\omega=da$ ,
$a\in A$ .
Consider the space  $\Omega^{1}_{A}/d\Omega^{0}_{A}$  of 1-forms on  $A$  modulo
the exact 1-forms. We can reduce any 1-form to an expression  $a\cdot db$  using the cyclicity. Next, modulo the exact forms  $a\cdot db+b\cdot da=0$ . Thus, there is a map of the space
$\Lambda^{2}(A)\to\Omega^{1}_{A}/d\Omega^{0}_{A}$  which is clearly surjective.
